opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we argue about a lot. I think the honest answer is that there's no single right form; it depends on what you mean by "human capabilities." But there are a couple of principles I keep coming back to.

The first is that the world is built for humans. Doors, stairs, tools, kitchens, factory workstations: they all assume a body of roughly our size, with two arms, hands at a certain height, and the ability to step over things and fit through narrow spaces. If you want a robot that drops into those environments without redesigning them, there's a strong argument for something roughly humanoid, or at least human-scale. That's a big part of why so many people are betting on humanoids right now.

That said, I'm a bit skeptical of copying the human body too literally. Evolution optimized us under constraints that don't apply to robots. Legs, for example: I've spent a lot of time on legged locomotion, and quadrupeds are just incredibly robust. They're statically stable, they recover from pushes easily, and they're much more forgiving to learn on. Bipeds are harder to control and more fragile when they fall. So if the task is mostly mobility over rough terrain, four legs, or even legs with wheels, can be strictly better than two.

Where the humanoid form really earns its keep is manipulation, and especially learning from humans. If your robot's body maps closely onto ours, you can use human demonstrations, teleoperation, and video data much more directly. That data advantage might matter more than any mechanical advantage, because right now data is the bottleneck.

So my view is: decide what capabilities actually matter, keep human scale and human-compatible reach so the robot fits our world, and stay pragmatic about the rest. Wheels where wheels work, legs where you need them, and hands that are capable but not necessarily anatomically perfect. With reinforcement learning and simulation, a lot of the control complexity is becoming manageable, so the question shifts from "can we control this body?" to "is this body worth the cost, robustness, and maintenance trade-offs?" That's where I think the real design decisions are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human-compatible scale and reach, and argues against copying human anatomy too literally. It does not define “humanoid” by capabilities rather than bodily resemblance.

r002.rationale: The response mentions narrow spaces and wheels, but does not identify the tradeoff between a larger wheeled footprint improving stability and limiting access through tight spaces.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I don't believe there's one right form, and I've become a bit skeptical of the framing that human capabilities require a human body. The argument you usually hear is that the world is built for humans, so a humanoid can use the same stairs, doors, tools, and so on, and that's a real argument. But if you look at what actually matters for most tasks, it's a much smaller set of things: you need to move through cluttered environments reliably, you need to manipulate objects at roughly human scale, and you need to do it safely around people. None of that strictly requires two legs and two arms.

My own background is in legged locomotion, mostly quadrupeds, and one thing we learned there is that the form factor you choose is really a trade-off between what's easy for the controller and what's easy for the task. A quadruped is quite forgiving. You can fall into a stable configuration, you have a lot of margin, and that means you can push the learning-based controllers very hard and recover from mistakes. A humanoid gives you much less margin. You're always balancing, the dynamics are faster and less stable, and small errors in perception or actuation become falls. So the humanoid is, in some sense, the hardest version of the problem, and you have to ask whether you're taking on that difficulty because the task demands it or because it looks like us.

Where I do think the humanoid form makes a strong case is on the data side. If we want robots to learn from human demonstrations, from video, from people teleoperating them, then having a body with a similar kinematic structure makes that transfer dramatically easier. The embodiment gap shrinks. So in a world where the bottleneck is data about how to do tasks, rather than the control itself, the humanoid starts to look much more rational than it did a few years ago.

I'd also push back a bit on treating form as fixed. A lot of what we see now is hybrid: a wheeled base with a humanoid torso, a quadruped with an arm. Those are often better engineering answers for a specific deployment. My feeling is that the field will converge on a few human-like forms because the economics of a common platform are so strong, not because it's optimal for any single task. And then the interesting work is in the controllers, because the controller is what makes a given body capable, and that's where learning has changed things the most.

r001.rationale: The response says human capabilities do not require a human body, but it does not define “humanoid” by capabilities rather than resemblance.

r002.rationale: It mentions wheeled bases as a hybrid form, but does not identify a footprint tradeoff between stability and access through tight spaces.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by human capabilities. If you mean a robot that can do useful tasks in the same environments as us, then it makes sense to have something roughly human-sized, with arms that can reach the same places and hands that can interact with the same objects. We've built our environments around our bodies, so that gives the humanoid form a practical advantage.

But that doesn't necessarily mean every robot needs to look exactly like a human. If you're working on a flat floor, wheels might be a much simpler solution than legs. Once you want to handle stairs, uneven terrain, or a wider range of environments, legs become more useful. So I would start with what we want the robot to do and let that guide the physical form. A humanoid is a compelling choice for a general-purpose robot, but it's not automatically the best choice for every task.

r001.rationale: The response frames a humanoid as useful for matching human environments and capabilities, and says it need not look exactly like a human.

r002.rationale: It compares wheels and legs by terrain and task, but does not mention a wheeled robot’s footprint trading stability against access through tight spaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right form depends on what you want the robot to do. If you have a very specific task, you can usually design a machine that does it more efficiently than a humanoid. You don’t necessarily need legs or two arms for that.

But if the goal is a robot that can do a broad range of things that humans do, then the human form becomes quite attractive. Our environments are built around us: the stairs, the doors, the tools, the heights of tables. A robot with roughly our dimensions and capabilities can potentially use all of that without us having to redesign the environment.

That doesn’t mean you have to copy every detail of the human body. The question is which features give you the versatility you need, and which just add complexity. Legs give you access to difficult terrain, hands let you interact with a wide variety of objects, but each of those also makes the control problem harder. So I would think about the capabilities first, and let those guide how humanlike the robot actually needs to be.

r001.rationale: The response says to prioritize the capabilities needed and not copy every human-body detail, framing how humanlike the robot should be by its capabilities rather than resemblance.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss wheeled robots, footprint, stability, or access through tight spaces.
